note: Vox-style rewrite of the v4 explainer (script_v4.md, 1:00 to 2:55): a hook, one person (Maya) through the product, then v4's business beats with v4's numbers. Product facts follow the live app: the real Copilot card on a $1,999 MacBook Pro on Amazon keeps the demo House down payment at risk (55–83% to 34–71%), and the Advisor answers a groceries question from the demo data. 'text' is said and captioned; 'say' (optional) is spelled for the AI voice. 'slot' is the shortest the beat may be; a longer take stretches it. Round 4: a dashboard tour beat (16), simpler competition, pricing and revenue lines.

gemini.direction: Narrate this like a warm, curious Vox explainer host: conversational and clear, a brisk, energetic pace with natural pauses, a slight smile, never salesy. Read exactly these words:

beats.text: Most money apps show you what already happened: last month's statement. But the decision happened at checkout.
Meet Maya. She's saving for a house, a trip to Japan and a rainy day. Then she spots a nineteen ninety-nine MacBook on Amazon.
Here's where our Copilot steps in. The Chrome extension sends just four things: price, store, item type and page type.
In about a second, a card appears: this MacBook cuts her odds on the house down payment, and suggests paying off a card first.
Why the house? Every goal draws from one pool of money, so one purchase moves them all, across five thousand simulated futures.
Her accounts live in one dashboard, and an AI Advisor answers from her own data. Code does the math; the AI only writes the words.
And it's all in one place: accounts, transactions, spending, goals, life events, investments and credit.
So who else does this? Monarch and Rocket Money track what you already spent. Projection Lab and Boldin plan ahead, if you go to them. None checks a purchase at checkout.
We do. FinVantage shows what one purchase does to every goal at once, and code checks every number, so the AI can't make one up.
We start with UTA students, then young professionals through the Chrome Web Store and creators, and later, banks and credit unions.
beats.say: We start with U.T.A. students, then young professionals through the Chrome Web Store and creators, and later, banks and credit unions.

beats.text: It's free with one linked account. Link multiple accounts and get the Copilot and the Advisor for ninety-nine dollars a year, after a free trial.

Here's the math. If a hundred fifty to four hundred fifty thousand people try it, and about one in ten keep paying, that's sixteen to forty-eight thousand members: one point six to four point eight million dollars a year.
After costs, each member brings in about seventy-two dollars a year.
Our ask: up to fifteen thousand dollars. Four thousand for security, three for legal, eight for the pilot.
By December third: ten UTA testers. Our target: six use it weekly, three say they'd pay.
beats.say: By December third: ten U.T.A. testers. Our target: six use it weekly, three say they'd pay.

beats.text: Security review first, then real banks. So Maya knows what a purchase does to her goals, before she buys.
